title: Report on Studying at National Taiwan University and the University of Freiburg
paragraphs: I spent two weeks, March 11 to 22, at National Taiwan University and twelve weeks, April 1 to June 21, at the University of Freiburg. At National Taiwan University I did clerkships in obstetrics and gynecology, and at the University of Freiburg in neurosurgery, anesthesiology, and obstetrics and gynecology.

Obstetrics and gynecology at National Taiwan University starts at 7:30. Obstetrics and gynecology each gather in separate meeting rooms and hold meetings. The meetings were attended by residents, interns and medical students, and were quite large. First there was sharing of information on inpatients and patients scheduled for surgery, followed by a mini-lecture by an intern. The explanations of the lectures were in Chinese, but the slides were all in English, so I could understand the content to some extent. In Taiwan, medicine is apparently basically learned in English, and the charts and surgical schedules were also written in English, which was a great help. Not only the morning mini-lectures but also at noon the residents introduced rare cases and papers, and many opportunities for presentations were provided, so I could sense that National Taiwan University is enthusiastic about education. After the meeting, regular work such as surgery begins. Before surgeries and individual procedures, the resident always carefully explained the patient and the content, which taught me a great deal. I was allowed to observe single-port laparoscopic surgery, prenatal diagnosis by level II ultrasound, infertility treatment, and urodynamic testing in urogynecology, all of which are hard to see in Japan, and it was a very valuable experience.

At the University of Freiburg, I did clerkships in neurosurgery at the university hospital, anesthesiology at Loretto Hospital and obstetrics and gynecology at St. Josef Hospital. The latter two hospitals are so-called external hospitals. Neurosurgery at the University of Freiburg is among the most famous in Germany, with around 15 operations a day, and doctors gather from all over Europe, so it was full of energy. The clerkship was mainly observing surgery, but the doctors willingly answered any question, and I learned a lot. The Loretto Hospital I visited next, in contrast to the university hospital, is a small hospital with about 300 beds. The only surgical departments were urology and orthopedics, and anesthesia was also given for the operations of these two departments. In Germany, specialty training starts immediately after graduation, so students are expected to acquire a certain number of procedures in clerkships before graduation. So in this clerkship I too experienced very many procedures, such as IV access, mask ventilation, intubation, anesthesia machine setup, spinal anesthesia and arterial line placement. When I told the doctor that I had never even placed an IV in Japan, he was very surprised, but he said "You will do it someday anyway, so try it for now," and taught me every procedure very carefully. Also, paramedic and anesthesia specialist nurse students were accepted here too, and everyone worked on procedures actively, which was a good stimulus. About anesthesia and the drugs used as well, the doctors answered any question in detail, and it was interesting to be able to learn about drugs that are not used in Japan. The last hospital where I did my clerkship, St. Josef Hospital, is a mid-sized hospital with 500 beds, and I spent the first two weeks in gynecology and the next two weeks in obstetrics. Every morning at 7:40 there was a joint obstetrics and gynecology conference, after which we split up to do our work. There are about 20 doctors, but most are women with children and they work in shared shifts, so there were only three to four each in obstetrics and in gynecology on any given day. The work of students here was blood sampling of postoperative and postpartum patients, IV access for preoperative patients, surgical assistance and so on, and when there was no surgery I was allowed to observe deliveries and outpatient clinics. There were many differences compared with obstetrics and gynecology in Japan, so it was very interesting. In natural deliveries, after birth the baby is taken to the mother's chest and held before the umbilical cord is cut, and in cesarean sections too the father is present and attends the baby's first examination, and I could not hide my surprise at situations I saw for the first time. I also learned many things impossible to experience in Japan, such as treatments different from Japan and the administration of drugs not approved in Japan, and it was a very meaningful clerkship. Finally, I sincerely thank Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川, everyone in the International Collaboration Office, the Student Affairs staff, and the professors of the University of Freiburg, who gave great support to make this study abroad possible. Thank you very much.
